steps.say: Undescended testis is common at birth and rare after infancy. About three in a hundred full term boys and up to thirty in a hundred premature boys are affected, because descent finishes late in pregnancy. Descent after three to six months is rare, so a testis still up at six months needs referral.
steps.tx: **Cryptorchidism** (undescended testis) affects about **3%** of full-term and up to **30%** of premature male newborns, since descent completes late in gestation. **Spontaneous descent** (unaided testicular drop) after **3 to 6 months** (three to six) is rare, so a testis still undescended at 6 months needs surgical referral rather than further waiting.

vis.alt: Illustration of milking technique with true versus ectopic testis map.
vis.caption: Examination maps true undescended versus ectopic testes before referral. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Surgery has a clock. Fixation between six and twelve months, finished by eighteen months, catches the months when germ cells still mature normally. Operating in this period protects sperm making and hormone cells, while delay trades fertility away and raises cancer risk.
steps.tx: Definitive **orchidopexy timing** (fixation scheduling) places surgery between **6 and 12 months** (six and twelve) of age, completed by **18 months** (eighteen), for **germ cell preservation** (protecting future sperm and Leydig cells). Operating in this window preserves spermatogenesis and Leydig architecture, while delay into childhood progressively sacrifices fertility and raises malignancy risk.

steps.say: A testis that cannot be felt is scoped, not scanned. Keyhole surgery is the gold standard test and treatment combined: it finds blind ending vessels proving a vanished testis, or locates a testis inside the tummy for same session fixation. Ultrasound adds nothing when nothing is felt.
steps.tx: **Diagnostic laparoscopy** (keyhole inspection) is the gold standard for the **non-palpable testis** (unfelt testis), combining diagnosis with treatment: it identifies **vanishing testis** (blind-ending vessels proving regression) or intra-abdominal localization for mobilisation in the same sitting. Ultrasound and MRI contribute nothing when nothing is palpable, and they delay the definitive look inside.

vis.alt: Illustration of empty scrotum with blind spermatic vessels and pituitary hormone rise.
vis.caption: Vanishing testis with blind-ending vessels as laparoscopy identifies it. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: High testes keep going on backup blood. The Fowler-Stephens operation cuts the main testicular vessels in one or two stages and relies on flow from the vas artery and groin muscle vessels. The testis lives on its secondary supply and reaches the scrotum without pulling, with staging in two sittings lowering shrinkage risk.
steps.tx: **Fowler-Stephens** orchiopexy (vessel-dividing fixation), single or two-stage, performs **testicular vessels ligation** (main vessel division) and relies on the **deferential artery collateral** (vasal artery backup) plus cremasteric vessels. The testis survives on secondary supply and reaches the scrotum without tension, with two-staging reducing atrophy risk.

steps.say: Undescended testes turn cancerous more often. Lifetime cancer risk rises four to eight fold, with seminoma the commonest type, and fixation fails to remove the risk. What surgery changes is detection: a scrotal testis can be felt, so tumours present earlier, and lifelong self checking stays mandatory.
steps.tx: **Malignancy risk cryptorchidism** (cancer risk in undescended testes) rises **4- to 8-fold** (four to eight times) lifetime, with **seminoma** (commonest germ cell tumour here) leading; orchidopexy facilitates examination but never eliminates risk. A scrotal testis can be felt by the patient, so tumours show earlier and smaller, and lifelong self-checks stay essential.

steps.say: A hernia sac almost always comes too. An open channel to the tummy persists in over ninety in a hundred cases, so every fixation includes high tying of the sac during open or keyhole repair. Missing the sac leaves a groin hernia that appears months later through the same cut.
steps.tx: **Patent processus vaginalis** (open peritoneal channel) persists in over **90%** (ninety in a hundred) of cryptorchid testes, requiring **hernia sac ligation** (high sac tying) during open or laparoscopic orchidopexy. Missing the sac leaves an indirect hernia presenting months later through the same groin.

Indirect hernia months later, same groin

steps.say: Two absent testes with normal male looks is an emergency until proven otherwise. Normally formed boys with no felt testes need immediate testing for salt losing adrenal overgrowth, plus chromosome testing and hormone stimulation. Missing the salt losing crisis kills within weeks, so fluids and steroids start on suspicion.
steps.tx: **Bilateral non-palpable testes** (both testes unfelt) with normal male genitalia demand urgent evaluation for **congenital adrenal hyperplasia** (CAH, salt-wasting enzyme defect), karyotype, and **hCG test** (hCG stimulation testing). A missed salt-wasting crisis kills within weeks, so steroids and fluids begin on suspicion while results pend.

steps.say: Hormones are not the answer. Hormone treatment with HCG or GnRH drugs is not advised as routine because lasting descent follows in under fifteen in a hundred, and treatment may harm future sperm cells. Surgery remains the standard, with hormones kept for highly selected retractile cases only.
steps.tx: **Hormonal therapy cryptorchidism** (drug-induced descent) with hCG or GnRH agonists is not routinely recommended given **low efficacy** (under **15%** durable descent, fifteen in a hundred) plus adverse effects on future germ cells. Surgery remains the standard; hormones serve highly selected retractile cases only, never as a substitute for timely orchidopexy.
